subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If f(x) = 1 + x + x² + x³ + ⋯ + x¹⁰⁰, find f′(1).

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.193, chapter 9 DIFFERENTIATION, Very Short Answer question 15(i). **Only the question was taken. The answer 5050 was checked before it was written: the derivative sum 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 100 was added directly and returned 5050, and a numerical difference quotient of the whole 101-term polynomial at x = 1 returned 5050.0004, the small excess being the curvature of a degree-100 polynomial over the step used.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what each term becomes after differentiating and what happens when you put x = 1.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Differentiate term by term
steps.margin_note: First mark. Differentiate the sum one term at a time using d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹. The constant 1 at the front differentiates to 0, so the first surviving term of f′ is the 1 that comes from x.
steps.memory_tip: Every power drops by one and the old power comes down in front, so the coefficients of f′ read 1, 2, 3 up to 100.
lines: Using d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹ on each term,

recall.must_convey: That term-by-term differentiation gives f′(x) = 1 + 2x + 3x² + ⋯ + 100x⁹⁹, with the constant giving 0.
accept: differentiate each term so it becomes one plus two x plus three x squared up to hundred x to the ninety nine
power comes down in front and drops by one

steps.why: Writing the derivative in full, with its first three terms and its last term, shows the pattern the second step depends on. Skipping straight to a number leaves nothing to mark.
common_mistakes: Writing the last term as 100x¹⁰⁰, forgetting that the power drops to 99.
Keeping the leading 1 in f′(x), so the sum comes out one too large.

steps.label: Put x = 1 and add 1 to 100
steps.margin_note: Second mark. At x = 1 every power of x is 1, so each term is just its own coefficient. The sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n+1)/2, with n = 100 here.
steps.memory_tip: 1 raised to any power is 1, so putting x = 1 leaves only the coefficients to add.
lines: Put x = 1. Every power of 1 equals 1, so each term reduces to its coefficient.
Sum of the first n natural numbers = n(n+1)/2, with n = 100

recall.must_convey: That at x = 1 the derivative is 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 100 = 100 × 101/2 = 5050.

steps.why: The sum formula is the whole point of the question. Adding 1 to 100 term by term would also reach 5050, but it is far slower than the single line n(n + 1)/2.
common_mistakes: Trying to add 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 100 one number at a time and running out of time.
Using n(n+1)/2 with n = 99, because the last derivative term shows x⁹⁹.

insider_note: Every power of 1 is 1, so f′(1) is just the sum of the coefficients 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 100. Use n(n+1)/2 rather than adding, giving 5050.
